question: What main body change causes widespread tissue lack of oxygen in blood disorders?

options.B: Reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood
options.D: Excessive production of white blood cells

explanation: Blood disorders often decrease red blood cells or hemoglobin, limiting the blood's ability to carry oxygen to tissues. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h1)

question: Why do blood disorders usually affect many parts of the body at the same time?

options.A: Because lymphatic vessels absorb toxins released by damaged erythrocytes
options.B: Because blood circulates through and nourishes every living tissue
options.C: Because bone marrow failure directly destroys all surrounding bone tissue
options.D: Because blood cells store excess glucose required by vital organs

explanation: Since the circulatory system reaches every part of the body, blood problems quickly show up as multi-organ issues. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h1)

question: What causes red blood cells to bend into a sickle shape in sickle cell disease?

options.A: Low oxygen tension causing hemoglobin polymerization
options.B: Excessive production of abnormal white blood cells
options.C: Rapid dehydration of blood plasma proteins
options.D: High concentrations of circulating serum iron

explanation: When oxygen levels drop, abnormal hemoglobin molecules stick together inside the red blood cell, pulling its flexible shape into a rigid crescent. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h2)

question: A patient with sickle cell disease reports sudden chest pain, fever, and a cough. Which problem should the nurse suspect first?
explanation: Chest pain, fever, and lung issues in sickle cell disease are classic signs of acute chest syndrome, which needs urgent care. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h2)

question: What is the medical term for bleeding directly into joint spaces in patients with clotting disorders?
explanation: Hemarthrosis means bleeding into joint cavities, a classic and painful problem seen in severe bleeding disorders like hemophilia. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h3)

question: Why do patients with very low platelets develop tiny spots and purple patches on the skin?

options.A: Because plasma proteins precipitate under the epidermal layer
options.B: Because white blood cells attack the superficial layers of skin
options.C: Due to the leakage of red blood cells from fragile microcapillaries
options.D: As a result of excessive iron deposition in subcutaneous tissue

explanation: Low platelet counts stop the body from fixing small blood vessel damage, causing tiny leaks of red blood cells into the skin. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h3)

question: What is often the only early sign of a serious infection in a patient with very low white blood cells?
explanation: Because these patients lack enough white blood cells to create pus or swelling, a fever is often the only warning sign of a dangerous infection. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h4)

question: How does the heart first try to make up for a severe lack of hemoglobin?

options.A: By increasing heart rate and stroke volume
options.B: By slowing down electrical conduction to rest
options.C: By constricting coronary arteries to save energy
options.D: By decreasing left ventricular muscle mass

explanation: To deliver enough oxygen when red blood cells are low, the heart beats faster and pumps harder. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h5)

question: What is the long-term heart problem caused by unmanaged, severe anemia over time?
explanation: Working extra hard for a long time to keep up circulation eventually wears out the heart muscle, leading to heart failure. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h5)

question: Why do patients who receive many blood transfusions end up with too much iron in the body?

options.A: Bone marrow actively manufactures excess storage proteins
options.B: The human body cannot actively excrete excess iron
options.C: The kidneys reabsorb all filtered iron from the urine
options.D: Transfused blood contains synthetic iron supplements

explanation: The human body has no natural way to get rid of extra iron, so frequent transfusions cause iron to build up in tissues. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h6)

question: Which vital organs are most easily damaged by a buildup of extra iron over time?
explanation: Extra iron tends to settle in the liver and heart muscle, causing serious damage if it is not removed. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h6)

question: What is the main danger when a blood clot breaks free from a deep vein in the leg?

options.A: It can travel to the lungs and cause a pulmonary embolism
options.B: It triggers immediate systemic bone marrow failure
options.C: It will dissolve immediately upon entering the arterial circulation
options.D: It causes localized skin necrosis at the site of origin

explanation: A loose clot can travel through the veins to the heart and get stuck in the lung arteries, blocking blood flow. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h7)

question: Why do conditions that cause too many red blood cells increase the risk of dangerous blood clots?

options.A: By increasing overall blood viscosity and slowing flow
options.B: By lowering the blood pressure to near-fatal levels
options.C: By destroying platelets before they can form plugs
options.D: By depleting the body of all circulating clotting factors

explanation: Having too many red blood cells makes the blood thick and slow, which makes it much easier for unwanted clots to form. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h7)

question: What is the most important first step when a patient with low white blood cells gets a new fever on the ward?

options.A: Administer an oral iron supplement to strengthen red blood cells
options.B: Wait four hours to see if the temperature resolves on its own
options.C: Encourage vigorous physical exercise to boost immune cell count
options.D: Report the finding and initiate prompt medical evaluation and cultures

explanation: A fever in a patient with low white blood cells is an emergency that often points to severe infection, needing quick tests and treatment. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h8)

question: A patient receiving a blood transfusion starts complaining of lower back pain and chills. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Document the mild reaction and continue observing the patient
options.B: Slow down the infusion rate and administer prescribed paracetamol
options.C: Stop the transfusion immediately and disconnect the tubing
options.D: Apply a warm compress to the patient's lower back area

explanation: Back pain and chills during a blood transfusion are warning signs of a bad reaction, and stopping the transfusion prevents further harm. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h8)
